title: How to Trim a Video With FFmpeg (and Prove the Cut Starts on the Right Frame)
author: Voor AI
summary: There are two ways to trim a video with FFmpeg, and they don't do the same thing: Fast, no re-encode: ffmpeg -ss 1 -i in.mp4 -t 2 -c copy out.mp4 . This is fast, but the video can only start on a keyframe . Exact, re-encode: ffmpeg -ss 1 -i in.mp4 -t 2 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -c:a aac out.mp4 . This starts on the frame you asked for, but the video is encoded again. Most "my trim is off by a second" bugs come from using the first command and expecting the second. Below, I trim a real clip both ways, measure which source frame each output really starts on, and turn the results into pytest checks you can keep in a media pipeline. Everything was run with FFmpeg 9.0.1 on macOS. The test clip The fixtures are three short AI-generated clips published as examples on Voor's Vidu Q3 page : 1952×1062, 30 fps, H.264 + AAC. These clips have very few keyframes, which makes the difference between the two methods easy to see. List the keyframes first: ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -skip_frame nokey \ -show_entries frame = pts_time -of csv = p = 0 vidu-q3-2.mp4 # 0.000000 # 2.200000 vidu-q3-2.mp4 (5.108 s, 153 frames) has only two keyframes, at 0.0 s and 2.2 s. vidu-q3-1.mp4 (4.11 s) has just one, at 0.0 s. That tells you in advance which cuts -c copy can make cleanly: almost none. The helpers All measurements come from ffprobe and from decoding frames, not from the command line we meant to run: def run ( cmd ): return subprocess . run ( cmd , capture_output = True , text = True ) def probe ( path ): r = run ([ FFPROBE , " -v " , " error " , " -show_entries " , " format=duration:stream=index,codec_type,codec_name,duration,nb_frames,start_time " , " -of " , " json " , str ( path )]) return json . loads ( r . stdout ) def keyframes ( path ): r = run ([ FFPROBE , " -v " , " error " , " -select_streams " , " v:0 " , " -skip_frame " , " nokey " , " -show_entries " , " frame=pts_time " , " -of " , " csv=p=0 " , str ( path )]) return [ float ( x . strip ( " , " )) for x in r . stdout . split () if x . strip ( " , " )] def frame_count ( path ): """ Frames a player will actually show (decoded, after edit lists). """ r = run ([ FFPROBE , " -v " , " error " , " -select_streams " , " v:0 " , " -count_frames " , " -show_entries " , " stream=nb_read_frames " , " -of " , " csv=p=0 " , str ( path )]) return int ( r . stdout . strip ()) To find out which source frame an output really starts on, decode both as tiny grayscale images and pick the closest match: def gray_frame ( path , index = 0 , size = ( 64 , 36 )): """ Decode one displayed frame as small grayscale bytes for comparison. """ w , h = size r = subprocess . run ([ FFMPEG , " -v " , " error " , " -i " , str ( path ), " -vf " , f " select=eq(n \\ , { index } ),scale= { w } : { h } ,format=gray " , " -fps_mode " , " passthrough " , " -frames:v " , " 1 " , " -f " , " rawvideo " , " - " ], capture_output = True ) return r . stdout def diff ( a , b ): """ Mean absolute pixel difference between two gray frames (0 = identical). """ return sum ( abs ( x - y ) for x , y in zip ( a , b )) / max ( 1 , len ( a )) def nearest_source_frame ( src , clip , clip_index = 0 , search = range ( 0 , 160 )): """ Index of the source frame that looks most like frame `clip_index` of `clip`. """ g = gray_frame ( clip , clip_index ) best , score = None , 1e9 for i in search : s = gray_frame ( src , i ) if not s : break d = diff ( g , s ) if d < score : best , score = i , d return best , score At 64×36 the comparison is cheap, and in this clip neighbouring frames differ enough that the best match is unambiguous. Re-encoded frames score about 0.1, unrelated frames score in the tens. Trim 1: stream copy def trim_copy ( src , dst , start , length ): """ Fast: no re-encode. Video can only begin on a keyframe. """ return run ([ FFMPEG , " -y " , " -v " , " error " , " -ss " , str ( start ), " -i " , str ( src ), " -t " , str ( length ), " -map " , " 0 " , " -c " , " copy " , " -avoid_negative_ts " , " make_zero " , str ( dst )]) I asked for 1.000 s → 3.000 s. What came back: Asked Got Duration 2.00 s 3.09 s Frames 60 92 First frame source frame 30 (1.000 s) source frame 0 (0.000 s) With -c copy FFmpeg can't create a new keyframe at 1.0 s, so the output starts at the previous keyframe, 0.0 s, and keeps everything up to 3.0 s. The cover image shows the difference: the frame you wanted is the mushrooms, the frame you got is the insect close-up from the start of the clip. Trim 2: re-encode def trim_exact ( src , dst , start , length , crf = 18 ): """ Frame-accurate: decode from the seek point and re-encode. """ return run ([ FFMPEG , " -y " , " -v " , " error " , " -ss " , str ( start ), " -i " , str ( src ), " -t " , str ( length ), " -map " , " 0 " , " -c:v " , " libx264 " , " -crf " , str ( crf ), " -preset " , " medium " , " -pix_fmt " , " yuv420p " , " -c:a " , " aac " , " -b:a " , " 160k " , " -movflags " , " +faststart " , str ( dst )]) Now the first frame matches source frame 30 (score 0.1), there are exactly 60 frames, and both audio and video streams last 2.000 s. The cost is encode time and one generation of quality loss. -crf 18 keeps that loss below what you'll notice on a clip like this, but it's still not a bit-exact copy. Trim 3: snap to a keyframe and copy If you don't need a specific frame, for example when cutting a preview or removing a slow start, move the cut to a keyframe and keep the speed of -c copy : def snap_to_keyframe ( path , start ): """ Latest keyframe at or before `start` - the only place stream copy can begin cleanly. """ ks = [ k for k in keyframes ( path ) if k <= start + 1e-6 ] return ks [ - 1 ] if ks else 0.0 snap_to_keyframe(clip, 2.5) returns 2.2. Copying from 2.2 s gives 62 frames that start exactly on source frame 66 (2.2 × 30), with no re-encoding. The rule is simple: stream copy is exact only when the start time is a keyframe. The -to trap -to is an output timestamp, so where you put -ss changes what it means: def trim_to ( src , dst , start , end , input_seek = True ): """ -to is an end *timestamp*; where -ss sits changes what that timestamp means. """ if input_seek : cmd = [ FFMPEG , " -y " , " -v " , " error " , " -ss " , str ( start ), " -i " , str ( src ), " -to " , str ( end )] else : cmd = [ FFMPEG , " -y " , " -v " , " error " , " -i " , str ( src ), " -ss " , str ( start ), " -to " , str ( end )] return run ( cmd + [ " -c:v " , " libx264 " , " -crf " , " 18 " , " -c:a " , " aac " , str ( dst )]) Command Duration ffmpeg -ss 1 -i in.mp4 -to 3 … 3.00 s (1.0 → 4.0 s) ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -ss 1 -to 3 … 2.00 s (1.0 → 3.0 s) With -ss before -i , the output clock restarts at 0, so -to 3 behaves like -t 3 . With -ss after -i , the timestamps stay on the source clock and -to 3 stops at 3.0 s. Output seeking decodes everything before the cut, so it's slower on long files. If you want an end time, the safest habit is to compute -t end-start yourself. The tests These are the checks I keep next to any trimming code. Each one encodes a fact measured above: import pytest import trim as T CLIP = " inputs/vidu-q3-2.mp4 " # 30 fps, 5.108 s, keyframes at 0.0 and 2.2 s ONE_GOP = " inputs/vidu-q3-1.mp4 " # 30 fps, 4.11 s, a single keyframe at 0.0 s FPS = 30 @pytest.fixture ( scope = " module " ) def out ( tmp_path_factory ): return tmp_path_factory . mktemp ( " trim " ) def test_fixture_keyframes (): assert T . keyframes ( CLIP ) == [ 0.0 , 2.2 ] assert T . keyframes ( ONE_GOP ) == [ 0.0 ] def test_stream_copy_starts_at_previous_keyframe ( out ): dst = out / " copy.mp4 " assert T . trim_copy ( CLIP , dst , 1.0 , 2.0 ). returncode == 0 first , _ = T . nearest_source_frame ( CLIP , dst , search = range ( 0 , 45 )) assert first == 0 # asked for 1.0 s, got the 0.0 s keyframe assert T . frame_count ( dst ) > 2.0 * FPS + 20 # and about a second of extra video def test_reencode_starts_on_requested_frame ( out ): dst = out / " exact.mp4 " assert T . trim_exact ( CLIP , dst , 1.0 , 2.0 ). returncode == 0 first , score = T . nearest_source_frame ( CLIP , dst , search = range ( 20 , 41 )) assert first == 30 and score < 1.0 # frame 30 = 1.000 s assert T . frame_count ( dst ) == 60 assert abs ( T . duration ( dst ) - 2.0 ) < 0.02 def test_audio_matches_video_after_exact_trim ( out ): dst = out / " exact-av.mp4 " T . trim_exact ( CLIP , dst , 1.0 , 2.0 ) s = { x [ " codec_type " ]: float ( x [ " duration " ]) for x in T . probe ( dst )[ " streams " ]} assert abs ( s [ " audio " ] - s [ " video " ]) < 0.05 def test_snapping_makes_stream_copy_clean ( out ): start = T . snap_to_keyframe ( CLIP , 2.5 ) assert start == 2.2 dst = out / " snap.mp4 " T . trim_copy ( CLIP , dst , start , 2.0 ) first , score = T . nearest_source_frame ( CLIP , dst , search = range ( 55 , 80 )) assert first == 66 and score < 0.5 # 2.2 s * 30 fps assert abs ( T . frame_count ( dst ) - 2.0 * FPS ) <= 2 def test_single_keyframe_clip_cannot_be_copy_cut ( out ): dst = out / " one-gop.mp4 " T . trim_copy ( ONE_GOP , dst , 1.5 , 1.0 ) first , _ = T . nearest_source_frame ( ONE_GOP , dst , search = range ( 0 , 60 )) assert first == 0 # whole GOP kept from the start @pytest.mark.parametrize ( " input_seek,expected " , [( True , 3.0 ), ( False , 2.0 )]) def test_to_depends_on_where_ss_is ( out , input_seek , expected ): dst = out / f " to- { input_seek } .mp4 " T . trim_to ( CLIP , dst , 1.0 , 3.0 , input_seek = input_seek ) assert abs ( T . duration ( dst ) - expected ) < 0.05 $ pytest -v test_trim.py test_trim.py::test_fixture_keyframes PASSED test_trim.py::test_stream_copy_starts_at_previous_keyframe PASSED test_trim.py::test_reencode_starts_on_requested_frame PASSED test_trim.py::test_audio_matches_video_after_exact_trim PASSED test_trim.py::test_snapping_makes_stream_copy_clean PASSED test_trim.py::test_single_keyframe_clip_cannot_be_copy_cut PASSED test_trim.py::test_to_depends_on_where_ss_is[True-3.0] PASSED test_trim.py::test_to_depends_on_where_ss_is[False-2.0] PASSED 8 passed in 15.14s Which one to use Exact frame matters (a cut on an action, a loop point, a clip that must be exactly N frames): re-encode. Speed matters and the start can move: snap to a keyframe, then -c copy . Never use a bare -ss … -c copy and assume the start is where you asked. Check the keyframes first. If you need -to , know which side of -i your -ss is on, or use -t . Limits Results are for FFmpeg 9.0.1 with MP4/H.264 input. Older builds and other containers handle copy-trims differently (some write an edit list that hides the extra frames in some players but not others), which is exactly why the tests decode frames instead of trusting the command. Frame matching by small grayscale images works when nearby frames differ. On a static shot, several frames will score the same, so check frame_count and timestamps instead. Re-encoding changes bitrate and quality. Pin -crf and -preset in the function so batches stay consistent. Generate a little extra, then trim AI video tools give you whole seconds, and the best moment rarely starts at 0.0 s. A practical workflow is to generate slightly longer than you need and trim with the exact method above. On Voor's Vidu Q3 generator the duration slider runs from 1 to 16 seconds, and the default 5-second 360p draft was quoted at 61 credits on 3 November 2026. That's enough to pick the best two-second window with trim_exact and keep the tests green.

title: Image to base64: when inlining helps and when it hurts
author: Dan Lumatic
summary: TL;DR Base64 turns every 3 bytes into 4 characters, about 33% bigger. On a gzipped response an image's penalty shrinks to about 1% (1.010x of the original in our test), but an uncompressed response pays the full third. Rule of thumb: inline only an icon of a few KB that your own code owns and uses once. Serve everything else as a file, because an inlined image re-downloads with every revision of the file that holds it. In the browser use FileReader.readAsDataURL . In Python use base64.b64encode(...).decode("ascii") . btoa throws on any character outside Latin-1. A reviewer writes "just base64 it", and the image moves into the file that holds it. It can no longer be cached on its own, it comes back with every deploy of that page, and it is a third bigger before compression. Nobody on the thread can say what the change cost, because the diff only shows a long string. Base64 adds a third; gzip hides it for images Every 3 bytes of input become 4 characters of output, so the encoded size is 4/3 of the original plus = padding to fill the last group ( RFC 4648 , section 4). We encoded random bytes in Python 3.14 to see the ratio. Padding adds at most two characters, which is why the smallest input is slightly worse and larger ones settle at 4/3: Original bytes Base64 bytes Ratio 1,000 1,336 1.3360x 10,000 13,336 1.3336x 100,000 133,336 1.3334x The usual objection is that gzip fixes this. For images it nearly does, on a compressed response. We used 50,000 random bytes as a stand-in for a PNG or JPEG, which are already compressed. As base64 they became 66,668 bytes. Gzip at level 9 shrank that text to 50,508 bytes, which is 1.010x the original binary. Gzip on the raw bytes gave 50,038 (1.001x). That ~1% figure holds for already-compressed images. An uncompressed API response, an email body or a stylesheet your server does not compress pays the full third. Even in the best case, gzipped base64 stayed above the raw size in our test, so inlining at most ties on bytes. SVG is the exception worth knowing. It is text, and a data URL does not require base64: the syntax is data:[<media-type>][;base64],<data> ( MDN ), so ;base64 is optional. In our reading, URL-encoding an SVG usually beats base64 because only the special characters grow. In our test a 13,800-byte SVG became 18,400 bytes as base64 (1.333x). Inline an image only if it is tiny, code-owned and used once Run each candidate through three questions: Is it small? Our rule of thumb is a few KB at most. That is a heuristic, not a measurement. A 16-pixel icon usually passes, and a photo almost never does. Does it change only when the file that embeds it changes? A logo mark in your CSS qualifies. A user avatar does not. Does it appear once? Each inline copy adds its full encoded size to the uncompressed file, to memory and to parse work. A compressed wire softens this, because gzip back-references the repeated copy. We embedded a 20,000-byte random payload as base64 once and it gzipped to 20,250 bytes. Embedded twice, it gzipped to 20,567 (1.016x), not 2.0x. You still ship the full size to anyone without compression. If any answer is no, serve a file. A file gets its own URL, its own cache entry and its own headers, and lazy loading can skip it entirely. Try this: search your stylesheets for url(data: and run each match through the three questions. Every hit that fails one should become a file. An inlined image re-downloads with every deploy An inlined image has no cache entry of its own. It lives inside its host: your HTML page, your CSS bundle or your JS bundle. Change one line of that file, deploy, and every returning visitor downloads the image again with it. A served file keeps its own entry and its own validators through all of those deploys. A data URL has neither. A quick piece of arithmetic, not a measurement: a 20,000-byte image inlined becomes 26,668 bytes. If its host file ships 10 times and a visitor returns after each deploy, that visitor downloads 266,680 bytes for an image that never changed. As a file, they download 20,000 bytes once. Compression shrinks the inlined number; the already-compressed file itself barely compresses at all. A data: URL is also an opaque origin. MDN states it directly: "Data URLs are treated as unique opaque origins by modern browsers" and "top-level navigation to data: URLs is blocked in all modern browsers". You cannot link to one as a page or open one in a new tab to debug it. If you run a Content Security Policy, img-src must also allow data: , and in our reading that allows every data image, not only yours. JavaScript: FileReader for files, TextEncoder before btoa For a user-selected file, let the browser do it: // `file` comes from <input type="file"> or a drop event const reader = new FileReader (); reader . onload = () => console . log ( reader . result . slice ( 0 , 40 )); reader . readAsDataURL ( file ); // data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSU We ran this in Chromium with a 1x1 PNG. reader.result is the complete data URL, ready for img.src . If you need only the base64 part, take everything after the first comma. btoa is the other tool people reach for, and it has a trap. It accepts only Latin-1 characters and throws on anything else: try { btoa ( " café ☕ " ); } catch ( e ) { console . log ( e . name ); } // InvalidCharacterError const bytes = new TextEncoder (). encode ( " café ☕ " ); console . log ( btoa ( String . fromCharCode (... bytes ))); // Y2Fmw6kg4piV The fix is to encode the text to UTF-8 bytes first, then turn each byte into one character for btoa . That is for strings. The spread in String.fromCharCode(...bytes) passes every byte as a function argument, so it suits short strings only. On Node v24.22.1 it worked with 120,000 arguments and threw RangeError at 200,000. For image files, skip btoa and use readAsDataURL . Python: b64encode returns bytes, so decode it import base64 raw = bytes ([ 0x89 , 0x50 , 0x4E , 0x47 , 0xFB , 0xFF , 0xFE ]) print ( base64 . b64encode ( raw ). decode ( " ascii " )) print ( base64 . urlsafe_b64encode ( raw ). decode ( " ascii " )) # iVBOR/v//g== # iVBOR_v__g== b64encode returns bytes , so .decode("ascii") gives you a string you can drop into an f-string such as f"data:image/png;base64,{encoded}" . The standard alphabet uses + and / . urlsafe_b64encode swaps them for - and _ (RFC 4648, section 5), which is what you want in a URL or a filename. Check the host file's size after every merge that touches images Inlining usually happens by accident: a bundler option, a loader default, a helpful teammate. The symptom is a host file that grows by about 4/3 of an image's size. Catch it in three steps: Record the size of your CSS and JS bundles on your main branch, for example wc -c dist/app.css . After a merge, compare. A jump close to 4/3 of some image's byte size means that image got inlined. Run it through the three questions above. If it fails one, extract it and serve it as a file. Put the size check in CI with a threshold, and the review comment stops being a guess about cost. Sourcing note: ratios and sizes come from random bytes encoded on Python 3.14 on 2026-11-02. The gzip repeat test and the spread limit ran on 2026-11-03 on Node v24.22.1, and the other snippets ran on Node 24, Chromium and Python 3.14. The HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 point, the cache and CSP points and the SVG advice are our reading of how browsers behave, and the deploy example is arithmetic. The opaque-origin and navigation quotes come from MDN.

title: Python Project Showcase: A 5-Month Journey to Building a Dashboard Boutique
author: Insights YRS
summary: Python Project Showcase: A 5-Month Journey to Building a Dashboard Boutique As a developer, there's no better feeling than seeing a project come to life after months of hard work and dedication. In this post, we'll dive into the story of Yann-Guibert's first Python project, a dashboard boutique built over the course of 5 months. We'll explore the challenges he faced, the lessons he learned, and the final product he's proud to share with the world. The Journey Begins Yann-Guibert, the creator of this project, started from scratch, with no prior experience in Python. He was determined to learn the language and build a project that would showcase his new skills. With a blank slate, he began by setting up his development environment, choosing the right tools, and planning his project. Setting Up the Environment Yann started by installing Python on his machine, along with a code editor and a version control system. He chose to use Visual Studio Code (VS Code) as his code editor, which he found to be highly customizable and feature-rich. For version control, he opted for Git, which he was already familiar with. Planning the Project Before diving into code, Yann took the time to plan his project. He decided to build a dashboard boutique, a web application that would allow users to browse and purchase various products. He created a rough outline of the features he wanted to include, such as user authentication, product management, and payment processing. The Challenges As Yann began building his project, he faced several challenges that tested his patience and skills. Here are a few of the most significant ones: Debugging and Troubleshooting As a beginner, Yann struggled with debugging and troubleshooting. He found it difficult to identify and fix errors in his code, which often resulted in frustration and wasted time. To overcome this, he learned to use the built-in Python debugger, pdb, and to read and understand error messages. Learning New Concepts Yann encountered many new concepts and technologies while building his project. He had to learn about web development frameworks, databases, and payment gateways, which was a steep learning curve. To stay organized, he created a list of topics he wanted to learn and tackled them one by one. Staying Motivated Building a project from scratch can be a daunting task, especially for a beginner. Yann faced moments of self-doubt and frustration, but he refused to give up. He set small goals for himself and celebrated each milestone, which helped him stay motivated and focused. The Final Product After 5 months of hard work, Yann's dashboard boutique is now complete. The application features a user-friendly interface, product management, and payment processing. Here are some of the key features: User Authentication The application includes user authentication, which allows users to create and manage their accounts. Yann implemented this feature using Python's built-in hashlib library and a simple password hashing algorithm. Product Management The dashboard boutique includes a product management system, which allows administrators to add, edit, and delete products. Yann used a combination of Python's sqlite3 library and the Flask web framework to build this feature. Payment Processing The application includes payment processing, which allows users to purchase products online. Yann implemented this feature using a third-party payment gateway and Python's requests library. Key Takeaways Yann's 5-month journey to building a dashboard boutique is a testament to the power of dedication and perseverance. Here are some key takeaways from his experience: Start small : Yann's project started with a simple idea, which he gradually built upon. This approach allowed him to focus on one feature at a time and avoid feeling overwhelmed. Learn from mistakes : Yann encountered many errors and bugs during his project, but he learned to use them as opportunities to improve and grow. Stay organized : Yann kept a list of topics he wanted to learn and tackled them one by one. This approach helped him stay organized and focused. Conclusion Yann's dashboard boutique is a remarkable achievement, considering he started from scratch with no prior experience in Python. His journey is a reminder that with dedication and perseverance, anyone can build a successful project. We hope his story inspires you to take on your own projects and challenges, and we look forward to seeing what you'll create next. Source: reddit.com

title: Mindful Screen Time Management: Mivo's Innovative Approach
author: Insights YRS
summary: Mindful Screen Time Management: Mivo's Innovative Approach In today's digital age, it's no secret that our reliance on screens has become a significant concern. With the constant stream of notifications, social media updates, and endless entertainment options, it's easy to get sucked into the vortex of screen time. However, excessive screen use can have detrimental effects on our mental and physical well-being, relationships, and overall quality of life. In response to this growing concern, Mivo has launched a new app that takes a unique, mindful approach to managing screen time. A New Era in Screen Time Management Mivo's innovative app is designed to help users develop a healthier relationship with their devices. Unlike other apps that might simply try to limit or restrict screen time, Mivo's approach is more holistic. By empowering users to take control of their screen time, the app encourages a deeper understanding of their habits and behaviors. This decision is not made for you, but by you. Mivo's app is designed to be a gentle reminder, rather than a strict disciplinarian. By giving users the power to choose, the app fosters a sense of responsibility and accountability. The Benefits of Mindful Screen Time Management So, what are the benefits of Mivo's mindful approach to screen time management? For starters, users can expect to: Develop a healthier relationship with their devices Reduce stress and anxiety associated with excessive screen use Improve their focus and concentration Enhance their overall well-being Gain a deeper understanding of their digital habits and behaviors Key Takeaways Mivo's new app is a game-changer in the world of screen time management. By taking a mindful approach, the app encourages users to become more aware of their habits and behaviors, ultimately leading to a healthier digital lifestyle. With its user-centric design and empowering approach, Mivo's app is poised to revolutionize the way we interact with our devices. What This Means In a world where screen time is increasingly becoming a dominant aspect of our daily lives, Mivo's app is a breath of fresh air. By promoting mindfulness and user awareness, the app is helping to shift the focus from mere screen time management to a more holistic approach to digital wellness. As we continue to navigate the complexities of the digital age, Mivo's app is a timely reminder that our relationship with technology is a two-way street – one that requires mutual respect, understanding, and responsibility. Conclusion Mivo's new app is a significant step forward in the quest for healthier screen time management. title: asyncpg + PgBouncer Transaction Mode: 61 Prepared Statement Errors
author: jidonglab
summary: On a weeknight around 9:40, fourteen people finished a session in my app inside the same three minutes. Three of them never got their report. The logs had the same line over and over: prepared statement "__asyncpg_stmt_1a__" already exists . I had added PgBouncer two days earlier to fix a connection limit problem. It fixed that one and introduced a new one. If you run asyncpg + PgBouncer transaction mode, this post is the autopsy I wish I had read first: why it fails only under load, why the obvious fix only gets you 85% of the way, and what actually got me to zero. TL;DR asyncpg uses named prepared statements ( __asyncpg_stmt_N__ ). Those live on one Postgres server connection. PgBouncer transaction mode hands your next transaction to whichever server connection is free. Your statement name is now on the wrong connection, or collides with someone else's. statement_cache_size=0 alone was not enough in my SQLAlchemy setup. Failures dropped from 61 to 9, not to 0, because SQLAlchemy's asyncpg dialect still calls prepare() with sequential names. The fix that worked: disable both caches and give every prepared statement a unique name with prepared_statement_name_func . Zero errors across the next 11,800 writes. Cost: p50 query time went from 3.1 ms to 3.6 ms because Postgres now re-parses every statement. I'll take it. What was the setup? The backend is FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2.x async, and asyncpg, talking to a managed Postgres instance with a hard cap of 100 connections. Each app worker held its own SQLAlchemy pool. Scale out to enough workers and the pools alone eat the cap, so I put PgBouncer in front in pool_mode = transaction . The system is Preterview, an interview practice app I run (full disclosure: I built it). A session is a live voice conversation, and when it ends the backend writes the transcript, per-question scores, and a written report in one burst of inserts. That burst is the write path that broke. Locally, everything passed. Staging passed. Production at quiet hours passed. The failures only showed up when a dozen sessions ended at once, which is exactly the moment you can't debug interactively. How bad was it? In the first 48 hours behind PgBouncer, out of 2,140 session-end writes: Error Count DuplicatePreparedStatementError: ... already exists 44 InvalidSQLStatementNameError: ... does not exist 17 Total failed writes 61 (2.9%) Every single failure happened when concurrent session-end writes were above roughly 20 in flight. Below that, zero. That pattern is the whole clue. Why does asyncpg break behind PgBouncer transaction mode? asyncpg breaks behind PgBouncer transaction mode because it prepares statements by name on a server connection, and PgBouncer doesn't promise you the same server connection twice. The statement name is client-side state pointing at server-side memory that may not be yours anymore. Here's the sequence in slow motion: Worker A runs INSERT INTO reports ... . asyncpg sends PARSE with the name __asyncpg_stmt_1a__ on server connection S1. Postgres stores it on S1. The transaction commits. PgBouncer returns S1 to its pool. Worker A's next transaction gets server connection S2. asyncpg's cache says "I already prepared this as __asyncpg_stmt_1a__ ", so it sends BIND with that name. S2 has never heard of it. "does not exist." Meanwhile Worker B, on its own fresh client connection, also counts from the same starting point. It lands on S1 and tries to PARSE a different query as __asyncpg_stmt_1a__ . S1 already has one. "already exists." With low concurrency, PgBouncer tends to hand back the same idle server connection, so the names line up by luck. Under load, connections get shuffled and the luck runs out. That's why it looked like a flaky bug instead of a configuration bug. The asyncpg error message even says this. The hint attached to the exception tells you that PgBouncer in transaction or statement mode doesn't support prepared statements properly and suggests statement_cache_size=0 . I had been reading only the first line of the traceback for two days. Does statement_cache_size=0 fix it? Partly. Setting statement_cache_size=0 stops asyncpg from reusing cached named statements across transactions, which kills most of the "does not exist" errors. In my setup it took failures from 61 to 9 over a comparable 48-hour window. Better, not fixed. First attempt: engine = create_async_engine ( DATABASE_URL , connect_args = { " statement_cache_size " : 0 }, ) The remaining 9 were all "already exists." The reason: SQLAlchemy's asyncpg dialect keeps its own prepared statement cache ( prepared_statement_cache_size ), and it calls asyncpg's prepare() explicitly. Explicitly prepared statements still get the sequential __asyncpg_stmt_N__ names. Two client connections counting from the same starting point, landing on the same server connection, still collide. So there are two caches and one naming scheme to deal with. I had fixed one cache. What is the fix for asyncpg + PgBouncer prepared statement errors? Disable both caches, and make every prepared statement name globally unique so collisions are impossible even when PgBouncer shuffles connections. SQLAlchemy 2.0 has a parameter built for exactly this: prepared_statement_name_func . from uuid import uuid4 from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine from sqlalchemy.pool import NullPool engine = create_async_engine ( DATABASE_URL , # points at PgBouncer, not Postgres poolclass = NullPool , # PgBouncer is the pool now connect_args = { " statement_cache_size " : 0 , # asyncpg's cache " prepared_statement_cache_size " : 0 , # SQLAlchemy's cache " prepared_statement_name_func " : lambda : f " __asyncpg_ { uuid4 () } __ " , }, ) Three changes, each for a separate reason: statement_cache_size=0 stops asyncpg from assuming a statement prepared earlier still exists. prepared_statement_cache_size=0 does the same for SQLAlchemy's layer. prepared_statement_name_func replaces __asyncpg_stmt_1a__ with a UUID. Two workers can no longer pick the same name, so "already exists" becomes mathematically boring. I also switched to NullPool . Running a SQLAlchemy pool on top of PgBouncer is double pooling: app-side connections sit idle holding PgBouncer client slots, and you get none of the multiplexing you added PgBouncer for. With NullPool , each checkout opens a cheap client connection to PgBouncer and closes it after. Result: 0 prepared statement errors across the next 7 days and 11,800 session-end writes , including two evenings with more than 30 concurrent writes. What does disabling prepared statements cost? Every query now gets parsed and planned fresh instead of reusing a plan. For my workload, short inserts and indexed lookups, p50 query time went from 3.1 ms to 3.6 ms and p99 from 14 ms to 17 ms. The session-end burst is about 40 statements, so that's roughly 20 ms added to a write the user never waits on. If your workload is heavy, repeated, complex queries, the parse cost could matter more. Measure your own p99 before and after rather than trusting my numbers. Is there a fix on the PgBouncer side? Yes. Newer PgBouncer versions (1.21 and later) can track protocol-level named prepared statements in transaction mode via max_prepared_statements . PgBouncer rewrites statement names and re-prepares them on whichever server connection you land on. I had to set it explicitly; it did nothing until I did. [pgbouncer] pool_mode = transaction max_prepared_statements = 200 I tested this on staging and it also got the errors to zero, with the plan-caching benefit back. I still ship the client-side config in production for one reason: my managed Postgres provider controls the PgBouncer version, and I don't want correctness depending on a setting I can't see. If you own your PgBouncer, the server-side option is the better long-term answer. What I'd check first next time Read the whole exception, including the hint. asyncpg told me the answer on day one. Reproduce with concurrency, not with retries. A single client never triggers this. I wrote a 40-coroutine script that fires the session-end write in parallel against staging PgBouncer, and it reproduced the bug in under a minute. Before that I had spent an evening adding retry logic, which turned 3% failures into 3% duplicate partial writes. Count your caches. asyncpg has one, SQLAlchemy has one. Any ORM wrapping a driver may add another. Never let session-level state cross PgBouncer transaction mode. Prepared statements are the famous one. SET without LOCAL , advisory locks, LISTEN , and temp tables break the same way. So why does asyncpg throw "prepared statement already exists" behind PgBouncer? Because asyncpg + PgBouncer transaction mode puts named, per-connection prepared statements on top of a pooler that reassigns server connections between transactions. Your statement name points at a connection you no longer own, or collides with another client's identical sequential name on the connection you got. The fix that took my production errors from 61 to 0: set statement_cache_size=0 and prepared_statement_cache_size=0 , give prepared statements unique names with prepared_statement_name_func (UUIDs work), and drop app-side pooling with NullPool . If you control PgBouncer 1.21+, max_prepared_statements solves it on the server side and keeps plan caching. Expect a small parse cost; mine was 0.5 ms at p50. Written by the developer behind Preterview , an interview prep platform.

title: Open Source Privacy Tools: Complete List 2026
author: Usman
summary: "Open source" is a verifiable claim — which means a list like this one is only worth publishing if someone actually verifies it. So in July 2026 we re-checked every tool on this page: license (OSI-approved or out), maintenance (a release or significant activity within 12 months), and governance (acquisitions, license changes, funding crises, project-status announcements). Several entries changed as a result, and we've said so rather than quietly rewording. That's also the honest pitch for open source itself: proprietary apps can promise zero tracking while quietly phoning home; public code can be checked. What follows is 34 tools across 11 categories that passed verification — plus, at the end, the open-source stack we run ourselves, because a list like this from a company that doesn't practice it would be decoration. In short 34 open source privacy tools across messaging, email, file sharing, analytics, VPN, browsers, passwords, cloud storage and photos, DNS blocking, operating systems, and search — every one license-checked and maintenance-verified in July 2026, with a country tag per tool. Start with Signal, Bitwarden, and Brave for immediate impact. All three are free. Updated 18 October 2026: we corrected the Pulse entry (the dashboard and tracker are open source, the backend runs as a managed service) and its script size, removed Nomad from the stack we run, and now describe Tessera as SDKs and a sidecar around opaque-ke. Update, 19-07-2026 — full re-verification of every entry. Notable changes: Session survived a serious funding crisis (note added), Briar entered maintenance mode, Bitwarden's enterprise modules moved to a source-available license (core stays open), Mullvad completed its OpenVPN retirement. Added: SimpleX Chat, Immich, Ente, Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, and a new DNS-blocking category. How We Verified This List Four criteria, applied to every entry in July 2026: Genuinely open source: an OSI-approved license (GPL, MIT, Apache, AGPL, MPL) for the product as you'd actually run it. Source-available licenses (BUSL, SSPL) don't qualify — see the FAQ for why that distinction has teeth. Active within 12 months: at least one release or significant development activity. Projects in formal maintenance mode are marked as such, not silently kept. Usable without expertise: a non-technical person should be able to install and use it (underlying protocols like WireGuard excepted). Governance noted: acquisitions, license moves, funding trouble, and controversies get a clause, not a cover-up. Trust survives bad news; it doesn't survive discovering the list glossed over it. Three tools on this list are ours (Pulse, and two entries in the "what we run" section). They're labeled. No tool paid for placement. What Are the Best Open Source Encrypted Messaging Apps? Signal — Best for Everyday Private Messaging Signal remains the gold standard: end-to-end encryption by default for messages, calls, and video, with the Signal Protocol so battle-tested that WhatsApp and Google Messages adopted it. Signal itself stores virtually no metadata — subpoena responses have shown account-creation date and last-connection date, nothing more. It's the team default at Ciphera. License: AGPL-3.0 · Country: US · Cost: Free · Platforms: All SimpleX Chat — Best for No-Identifier Messaging SimpleX goes a step further than everyone else in this category: no phone number, no email, and — uniquely — no user identifiers of any kind, not even random ones. Message queues are unidirectional and disposable, so there's no stable "you" for servers to correlate. Actively developed and audited; the most interesting new entrant since our last revision. License: AGPL-3.0 · Country: UK · Cost: Free · Platforms: iOS, Android, desktop Element (Matrix) — Best for Decentralized Team Communication Element runs on the Matrix protocol — a federated network where you control your own server. The French and German governments run internal messengers on Matrix (Tchap, BwMessenger). If any single operator disappears, the network keeps running. License: AGPL-3.0 / GPL-3.0 (commercial licensing available) · Country: UK · Cost: Free self-hosted; hosted plans available · Platforms: All Session — Best for Anonymous Messaging Session requires no phone number or email, and routes messages through an onion network that hides metadata even from relay servers. One honest note from our verification: the foundation behind it nearly shut down in mid-2026 after a funding crisis, surviving on roughly $1M in community donations. The project is alive and shipping, but running leaner than before — worth knowing if you're betting a workflow on it. License: GPL-3.0 · Country: International (foundation) · Cost: Free · Platforms: All Briar — Best for Extreme Conditions Briar syncs peer-to-peer over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi — no internet required, no servers at all — which makes it unique for internet shutdowns and extreme-risk situations. Verification note: Briar formally entered maintenance mode in July 2026 (security fixes only, no new features). For its niche, that's acceptable; for a daily driver, pick Signal or SimpleX. License: GPL-3.0 · Country: UK · Cost: Free · Platforms: Android What Are the Best Open Source Private Email Providers? Proton Mail — Best for Encrypted Email Proton Mail offers end-to-end encryption between Proton users and zero-access encryption for stored mail, under Swiss jurisdiction, with fully open-source clients. Over 50,000 business customers as of 2026. It's the benchmark for private email, and what several of us use personally. License: GPL-3.0 (clients) · Country: Switzerland · Cost: Free tier; paid from $3.99/mo · Platforms: All Tuta — Best for Post-Quantum Email Tuta has run hybrid post-quantum encryption (TutaCrypt) in production since 2024 — earlier than nearly anyone — and encrypts subject lines, which Proton doesn't. German-hosted and expanding (a government-grant-funded encrypted drive is in beta). License: GPL-3.0 · Country: Germany · Cost: Free tier; paid from EUR 3/mo · Platforms: All Thunderbird — Best Desktop Email Client Thunderbird keeps a local, open-source client viable in a webmail world: any provider, built-in PGP, active 2026 roadmap (Exchange support, database overhaul) under Mozilla subsidiary MZLA. License: MPL-2.0 · Country: US · Cost: Free · Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux What Are the Best Open Source Encrypted File Sharing Tools? Send — Best for Self-Hosted File Transfers Send is the community fork of Mozilla's discontinued Firefox Send: end-to-end encrypted transfers with expiring links, self-hostable. Caveat from verification: the flagship public instance is a single-maintainer community project — self-host it if you need it to exist next year. License: MPL-2.0 · Country: Netherlands (maintainer) · Cost: Free self-hosted · Platforms: Web OnionShare — Best for Anonymous File Sharing OnionShare serves files directly from your machine over Tor — no server ever holds the file, and the share vanishes when you close the app. Still actively released. License: GPL-3.0 · Country: International · Cost: Free · Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux What Are the Best Open Source Privacy-First Analytics Tools? For the detailed comparison of this category, see Pulse vs Google Analytics vs Plausible vs Fathom . Pulse — Best for Zero-Cookie Analytics Pulse — ours, so judge accordingly — collects website analytics with no cookies and no fingerprinting, and never stores IP addresses. The dashboard and tracking script are open source, while the backend runs as a managed service. The script is under 3 KB gzipped, data lives in Switzerland, and in our view Pulse needs no consent banner. License: AGPL-3.0 (dashboard and tracker) · Country: Belgium (company) / Switzerland (data) · Cost: Free tier · Platforms: Web Plausible — Best Lightweight Analytics Plausible pioneered the category: a sub-2 KB script, simple dashboard, EU hosting, no cookies. The Community Edition is self-hostable. License: AGPL-3.0 · Country: Estonia · Cost: From $9/mo cloud; free self-hosted · Platforms: Web Umami — Best for Self-Hosted Simplicity Umami is MIT-licensed, deploys via Docker in minutes, and has become the default "just give me pageviews on my own server" choice. License: MIT · Country: US · Cost: Free self-hosted · Platforms: Web Matomo — Best Full Google Analytics Replacement Matomo is the mature heavyweight: funnels, heatmaps, tag management — the full GA feature set with complete data ownership. License: GPL-3.0 · Country: New Zealand · Cost: Free self-hosted; cloud from EUR 23/mo · Platforms: Web What Are the Best Open Source VPN and Network Privacy Tools? Mullvad — Best No-Nonsense VPN Mullvad completed its OpenVPN retirement in January 2026 and now runs WireGuard-only. EUR 5/month flat, no email required, cash accepted by post, apps open source and independently audited, and a documented history of having nothing to hand over. License: GPL-3.0 (apps) · Country: Sweden · Cost: EUR 5/mo · Platforms: All ProtonVPN — Best Free-Tier VPN ProtonVPN 's free tier has no data caps and no ads — genuinely usable rather than a crippled demo — and Secure Core multi-hops traffic through hardened data centers. License: GPL-3.0 (apps) · Country: Switzerland · Cost: Free tier; paid from $4.99/mo · Platforms: All WireGuard — Best VPN Protocol WireGuard is the protocol underneath the good VPNs: ~4,000 lines of code versus 100,000+ for OpenVPN, in the Linux kernel since 5.6. If you run your own server, this is the primitive to build on. License: GPL-2.0 · Country: — · Cost: Free · Platforms: All major OS What Are the Best Open Source Privacy Browsers? Firefox — Best Independent Browser Firefox remains the only major browser whose engine isn't Chromium — an independence that matters for the whole web, not just your tabs. Worth one clause of honesty: Mozilla's early-2025 Terms-of-Use wording sparked a real backlash before being walked back; the product's tracking protection is unchanged and strong. License: MPL-2.0 · Country: US · Cost: Free · Platforms: All Tor Browser — Best for Anonymity Tor Browser routes traffic through three relays with fingerprinting defenses layered on Firefox ESR. Slower, by design, in exchange for genuine anonymity. Note: US government funding cuts in 2025 hit the project's budget — the software is unaffected, but it has never needed community support more. License: BSD-3-Clause (Tor) / MPL-2.0 (browser base) · Country: US (non-profit) · Cost: Free · Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android Brave — Best Privacy-by-Default Browser Brave blocks ads and trackers out of the box on a Chromium base (full extension compatibility), with 100M+ monthly users as of late 2025. Its crypto features are ignorable if they're not your thing. License: MPL-2.0 · Country: US · Cost: Free · Platforms: All LibreWolf — Best for Firefox Purists LibreWolf is Firefox with every telemetry and sponsorship surface removed, tracking Firefox ESR within days of each release. License: MPL-2.0 · Country: — · Cost: Free · Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux What Are the Best Open Source Password Managers? Bitwarden — Best Overall Password Manager Bitwarden is cross-platform, regularly audited, self-hostable, and the free tier genuinely covers individual use. Verification nuance: the core clients and server remain GPL/AGPL, but newer enterprise modules ship under a source-available "Bitwarden License," and January 2026 brought a steep premium price hike — on top of private-equity investment taken back in 2022. The open-source core is unaffected today — we're noting the trajectory, not sounding an alarm. License: AGPL-3.0 (server), GPL-3.0 (clients), source-available enterprise modules · Country: US · Cost: Free; premium $10/yr · Platforms: All KeePassXC — Best Offline Password Manager KeePassXC keeps your vault in an encrypted local file you control — no cloud, no account, no company. Pair with Syncthing or Nextcloud for multi-device sync on your own terms. License: GPL-2.0 / GPL-3.0 · Country: — · Cost: Free · Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux What Are the Best Open Source Cloud Storage and Photo Tools? Nextcloud — Best Self-Hosted Cloud Platform Nextcloud is the full Google-Workspace replacement — files, calendar, video calls, document editing — self-hosted, with strong momentum from European governments' sovereignty push in 2025–2026. License: AGPL-3.0 · Country: Germany · Cost: Free self-hosted; enterprise plans · Platforms: All Cryptomator — Best Encryption Layer for Any Cloud Cryptomator adds client-side encryption on top of whatever cloud you already use — the vault syncs like a normal folder, but the provider sees only ciphertext. License: GPL-3.0 · Country: Germany · Cost: Free desktop; paid mobile · Platforms: All Immich — Best Self-Hosted Photo Library Immich is the credible self-hosted Google Photos replacement — mobile backup, timeline, search, face grouping — developed full-time under the FUTO umbrella and improving at a startling pace. The standout addition to this list in 2026. License: AGPL-3.0 · Country: US (FUTO) · Cost: Free self-hosted · Platforms: Server + iOS/Android Ente — Best Encrypted Photo Cloud Ente offers end-to-end encrypted photo storage if you'd rather not run a server — and its companion app, Ente Auth, is an excellent open-source 2FA authenticator, filling a category this list previously lacked. License: AGPL-3.0 · Country: India · Cost: Free tier; paid plans · Platforms: All What Are the Best Open Source DNS-Level Blockers? New category this revision — network-level blocking protects every device behind it, including the ones (TVs, IoT) that can't run a browser extension. Pi-hole — Best for the Home Network Pi-hole sinkholes ad and tracker domains for your entire network from something as small as a Raspberry Pi. The classic homelab first project, still actively maintained. License: EUPL-1.2 · Country: — · Cost: Free · Platforms: Linux (incl. Raspberry Pi) AdGuard Home — Best Polished Self-Hosted DNS Filter AdGuard Home covers the same ground as Pi-hole with a more polished UI and built-in encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) upstream support. The Home product is fully open source (the company also sells proprietary apps — don't conflate them). License: GPL-3.0 · Country: Cyprus · Cost: Free · Platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows, ARM What Are the Best Open Source Private Operating Systems? GrapheneOS — Best Secure Mobile OS GrapheneOS hardens Android for Pixel devices — memory-safety mitigations, sandboxed Google Play compatibility, no Google services by default. It gained its first major OEM partnership in 2026, a strong signal for longevity. License: MIT / Apache-2.0 · Country: Canada · Cost: Free · Platforms: Google Pixel Tails — Best Amnesic Live OS Tails boots from USB, routes everything through Tor, and forgets everything at shutdown. Actively released (7.x series through 2026), and still what journalists reach for. License: GPL-3.0+ · Country: — · Cost: Free · Platforms: Any PC via USB QubesOS — Best Compartmentalized Desktop QubesOS isolates every application in its own virtual machine — a compromise in one compartment stays in that compartment. Demanding, and worth it for high-risk work. 4.3 shipped in December 2025, with 4.3.1 following in June 2026. License: GPL-2.0 · Country: Poland (origin) · Cost: Free · Platforms: x86 desktops What Are the Best Open Source Private Search Engines? SearXNG — Best Self-Hosted Search SearXNG aggregates results from dozens of engines without any of them knowing who searched. Run your own instance or use a public one. License: AGPL-3.0 · Country: — · Cost: Free · Platforms: Web (self-hosted or public instances) Brave Search — Best Independent Index Brave Search built its own index — no Google or Bing dependency, a feat only a handful of companies have managed — and it's now genuinely independent at 40B+ pages. The index is proprietary; it earns its slot here for independence and no user tracking, clearly labeled. License: Proprietary index, open-source browser · Country: US · Cost: Free; premium $3/mo · Platforms: Web The Open-Source Stack We Run Ourselves A list like this is cheap if the publisher's own stack is a black box. Ours is partly open: the Pulse dashboard and tracker, Tessera and Sigil are public, while the Pulse backend runs as a managed service. What Ciphera ships and runs: Software Role License Tessera (ours) SDKs and a sidecar around opaque-ke, Meta's OPAQUE library: the system behind our login Apache-2.0 Sigil (ours) SSRF-hardened favicon resolution service Apache-2.0 Pulse (ours) Cookieless analytics (listed above); the dashboard and tracker are open source, the backend is a managed service AGPL-3.0 Stalwart Self-hosted mail server (Community Edition) AGPL-3.0 Woodpecker CI All our build and deploy pipelines Apache-2.0 Traefik Reverse proxy as our cluster ingress MIT Prometheus + Alertmanager Metrics and alerting Apache-2.0 Grafana + Loki Dashboards and logs AGPL-3.0 PostgreSQL The database behind most of our services PostgreSQL License And the honesty beat, because the source-available distinction cuts against us too: we also run HashiCorp Vault, which is BUSL-licensed (source-available, not open source), and Teleport, whose repository is AGPL but whose binaries carry usage restrictions since v16. We know the difference, we count them accordingly, and they're on the long-term replacement list. If a vendor's "open source" page doesn't make these distinctions, that tells you something about the rest of the page. Which Three Should You Start With? You don't need 34 tools. Start with Signal for messaging, Bitwarden for passwords, and Brave or Firefox for browsing — the three categories where the most personal data actually leaks, all free, all installable this afternoon. From there: Proton Mail for email, Pi-hole for the whole household, Nextcloud when you're ready to own your cloud. Every claim on this list can be checked against public sources, and where part of a product is closed (for example Brave Search's index or Pulse's backend) the entry says so. That is the entire point: privacy you don't have to take on faith .

title: A practical GIF and PNG check for transparent game characters
author: liangqi zhao
summary: A character can look smooth in transparent PNG frames but develop jagged edges or speckled colour in an animated GIF. This is not necessarily a broken source image: the formats preserve different information. Check the intended delivery format before polishing individual frames. What each format can preserve A PNG frame can store a full alpha channel, so an edge pixel can be partly transparent. GIF uses indexed colours and a designated transparent palette index; a pixel is either transparent or not. Each colour table has at most 256 entries. An encoder may use different palettes or frame rectangles, so do not assume the entire animation necessarily shares one simple global palette. The MDN image-format guide explains the format constraints. The practical consequence: a GIF made from soft, antialiased frames must approximate partial transparency. An encoder may use a threshold, a matte or dithering; the exact result depends on its settings. A matte chosen for a dark page can produce an edge halo on a light page. A repeatable comparison Keep the original transparent PNG frames and make a separate GIF preview. Do not overwrite the source frames. Preview both over black, white and a representative game background. Inspect hair tips, feathers and translucent effects as well as broad body areas. Play the GIF at its intended size and speed. Dithering or palette changes that are unobtrusive in one frame can shimmer between frames. If the destination supports it, compare a lossless animated format with alpha, such as APNG, or ship the PNG frames or sprite sheet to the game instead. Confirm the target engine and browser support before choosing a format. Recheck timing and looping after export: the preview is a separate artifact and can behave differently from the runtime animation. For native pixel art, preserve the intended limited palette and hard transparency; avoid smoothing or adding half-transparent pixels merely to make a preview appear larger. For painted 2D art, preserving soft edges may be more important than GIF compatibility. MotifDeck is an AI game-art workspace where creators can inspect transparent extracted character frames and choose their timing. These format checks apply regardless of how the frames were made. By Allen Zhao for MotifDeck, with AI assistance. The author is affiliated with MotifDeck.

title: Why banks block AI agents at the login
author: Dan Lumatic
summary: TL;DR A bank login carries only a password, so an agent using your password and a thief using a phished one look identical, and the bank refuses both. Charles Schwab says a given agent might hit its login "30, 40, 50 times" a week and gets blocked. Bank of America's customer email and Wells Fargo's Nov 24 account terms can leave the customer responsible for what an agent does with their password. Read-only access the bank approves is open today. Moving money needs credentials issued to the agent, and the US rule meant to replace password-based access is frozen in court. Bank of America emailed customers a message titled "Protecting your finances in the AI world," telling them not to share passwords with AI agents. If they do, the email says, they are "responsible for activity resulting from that access." If you build agents that touch customer accounts, this is likely why your login-based demo gets blocked. From the bank's side of the glass, a logged-in agent and a stolen session are the same thing, so banks refuse the login and leave the customer responsible for whatever slips through. A bank login cannot tell your agent from a phished password A login checks one thing: whether the password matches the one the bank has on file. The customer, the customer's agent and a criminal with a phished password all present the same proof. Axios reported on Oct 22 , citing people familiar with the matter, that banks "were detecting outside AI agents inside customer accounts", including some "that attempted actions that appeared independent of their users' instructions". AI News adds a counterpoint: Morgan Stanley, which has blocked third-party agents, "had not seen any unauthorised or rogue instances," a person familiar with the bank told Reuters. The agents in question are consumer tools such as Meta's Muse, which can connect to accounts with a customer's authorization to monitor balances and transactions. To the bank, an agent's login is a correct password from a device it has never seen, which is also how a criminal's login looks. The one defense available at that door is to refuse it. Schwab's CEO says the firm is "keeping rogue agents from being able to log in on the client's behalf." The blocks show a bank can spot agent-like traffic. A blocked attempt still says nothing about whose agent it was, because the password is all the form carries. That is our reading of the evidence; no bank states it in these words. Read-only access the bank approves is open today Axios reported that most banks have approved, or are moving toward, read-only access that lets an agent view account information without moving money. Schwab plans to let outside AI models check balances and research through its own MCP servers, but not move money: "We control the authentication experience." These agents arrive through a path the bank built, so the bank can recognize them and the identity question never comes up. Try this: Check how your integration connects to the bank. If it asks users for a bank username and password, expect trouble: Schwab blocks agent logins, and TD tells clients never to share their log-in credentials with an AI agent. If it connects through the bank's own approval and only reads balances and transactions, it uses the access banks already approve. Bank of America and Wells Fargo put the liability on the customer TechCrunch, reporting on the Bank of America email, puts the general rule this way: "Account agreements at most banks hold customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to." Wells Fargo is writing it down for agents. As AI News summarizes it, the updated Online Access Agreement, effective Nov 24, says that, subject to applicable law, instructions and transactions from an agent given a customer's login details or authority "can be treated as the customer's own without further verification." Customers are also made responsible for unintended actions and for actions that exceed the authority they gave. For a builder, that means the customers using a login-based integration are told not to share credentials, the bank may block the login, and the customer can carry the risk if something goes wrong. Where each bank stands Per reporting through Nov 1: Bank What it does On the record JPMorgan Chase Blocks external agents from acting for retail customers; some third-party tools view data only Spokeswoman to CNBC; Bloomberg Bank of America Imposed limits on agents Customer email warning (TechCrunch, Oct 27) Wells Fargo Restricts third-party agent access Nov 24 agreement (AI News) Charles Schwab Blocks agent logins; outside AI models connect on its terms, no money movement CEO Rick Wurster: agents blocked from logging in on clients' behalf (InvestmentNews, Oct 28) BMO, CIBC, RBC, TD, Scotiabank Four block personal AI agents; Scotiabank limits third-party agents while it monitors TD's advice: keep log-in credentials away from AI agents (CBC, Oct 29) Moving money needs agent-scoped credentials; the rule meant to replace password sharing is frozen An agent a bank could admit would carry a credential of its own, scoped to specific permissions, revocable without touching the customer's login, with liability set in advance. OAuth-style tokens show the shape: an app acts for you within a limited scope you can cancel without changing your password. As AI News reports, relaying American Banker, the Personal Agent Protocol is an open standard led by Sierra and Meta that "sets out how personal AI agents identify themselves to businesses, establish whom they represent and limit their access to what the customer has authorised". It is built on OAuth, and the customer decides whether an agent gets read-only or write access. Bank of America, BBVA, Synchrony and Wells Fargo have joined it, even as Bank of America and Wells Fargo restrict the credential-based agents already in use. The US rule in the picture is the CFPB's Section 1033 open banking rule, finalised in October 2024 and meant to replace credential-based access. As AI News reported, the rule "requires banks to maintain a developer interface, typically an API, through which authorised third parties can access customer data", and "bars banks from relying on a third party's use of customer credentials" to reach that interface. A federal court has enjoined the CFPB from enforcing it, and as of August 2026 a revised proposal had gone to White House review without being published. As AI News put it: "With the rule on hold, there is no regulated route for AI agents into bank accounts." Two things to watch: Whether Bank of America or Wells Fargo accept write-capable agents under the protocol, since membership signals a commitment to agent identity and a customer-chosen write option. Whether the revised Section 1033 rule gets published, since it would give agents a regulated way in without a password. Until a bank can issue an agent credentials of its own, a logged-in agent and a stolen session look the same from the bank's side, so expect the login to stay closed. If you build anything that touches customer accounts, build for the read-only lane the bank approves. title: A Practical DIY SEO Audit: A Checklist for Small Websites
author: Евгений Брусницын
summary: An SEO audit is useful when it produces a list of observable problems, owners and ways to verify the fixes. A score from one tool is not the outcome. Start with important pages: can people open them, navigate to them and complete their task? Then investigate crawl and indexing signals, content, internal links and mobile usability. This walkthrough is designed for an initial audit of a small site. A large migration, complex catalogue or major traffic loss may require deeper investigation with developers and search specialists. An audit creates testable hypotheses; it does not guarantee higher rankings. 1. Define the scope and baseline Write down the goal, domain, target audience, region and observation period. For example, you may want to verify important service pages after a redesign. Compare equivalent periods where possible and note seasonality, advertising and changes to the site. Select the home page, priority services or categories, a few product pages, articles and known problem URLs. On a large site include examples of different templates, filters and pagination. A sample can reveal recurring patterns but is not a complete URL inventory. If available, use your search-engine webmaster accounts, site analytics and a crawler. Without account access, begin with manual browser checks and clearly record what you cannot establish. A search operator or an external test is not a complete list of indexed URLs. Create a working table with the URL or template, observation, evidence, date, likely impact, owner, task and retest status. Do not put passwords or visitors' personal information into it. 2. Check access and responses Open selected URLs in ordinary and private browser windows, on desktop and mobile. Is the main content visible without an unexpected login? Do important links reach their stated destination? Test forms in an appropriate safe way and compare the address before and after navigation. Use a diagnostic tool or ask a developer to inspect HTTP responses. A page that exists should normally return a successful response; a redirect should lead to an appropriate final URL. Investigate server errors and long redirect chains. Do not redirect every missing URL to the home page merely to make a report look cleaner. Agree on the preferred host and protocol with the team. Check whether internal links and redirects consistently lead there. Before changing server rules, map affected addresses, test the change and prepare a rollback. 3. Investigate crawling and indexing In the relevant webmaster tools, inspect several priority URLs. Look at whether the system knows the page, the reason given for any exclusion and the date of the available information. Reports may update at different times, so compare them with the current page and recent changes. Check for login requirements, network restrictions or robot rules that might block important public content. A robots.txt restriction controls crawling; blocking a URL from crawling is not the same as reliably removing it from an index. Consider a noindex directive in the context of whether a crawler can access the page to see it. Consult the current documentation for the relevant search engine before making changes. Do not open private or administrative areas just to reduce the number of warnings. Determine why a restriction exists and involve the responsible developer. If an important URL is absent from search, test more than one possible explanation: accessibility, crawl permissions, content, links and canonical signals. Record what each test establishes and what remains uncertain. 4. Compare sitemaps and preferred URLs Find the XML sitemap actually used by the site and open it. Sample addresses from multiple sections. Compare sitemap URLs with their final destinations after redirects and with internal links. Do not indiscriminately include every filter or administrative URL without deciding whether it belongs there. Where a canonical link is present, check that its target exists and corresponds to the content. A canonical is a signal of a preferred version, not a guarantee that a search engine will select it. Similar templates do not automatically make distinct products or articles duplicates. Look for conflicting signals among navigation, sitemaps, redirects and canonical links. After a template fix, verify representative real URLs rather than assuming the setting resolved every case. 5. Follow the user's path Choose an important service or article and try to reach it through the menu, its section and related pages. Is the path understandable without searching the site? Record broken links, pages without meaningful internal links and anchor text that does not describe its destination. Do not link every page to every other page. A relevant link is one that helps a reader move from a question to the next useful answer. Update links when their destination changes or no longer delivers what the text promises. For each priority page, write down the reader's question and expected action. A service page needs useful conditions and a next step; a tutorial needs prerequisites, steps and limits. Check whether the title promises a comparison or checklist that the content fails to provide. Review facts, contact details and images for accuracy. Similar queries or headings are a reason to compare page purposes, not automatic proof that one URL should be deleted. Before consolidation, consider inbound links, analytics and a redirect plan. 6. Check mobile usability and performance Use a real phone where possible. Check readable text, navigation, forms, tap targets and tables. Pop-ups should not prevent access to the main content. Review several templates, not just the home page. Combine available real-user data with a lab performance test. Record the URL, device, conditions and date: a single run depends on the network and environment. Investigate large images, third-party scripts, delays and unexpected layout movement, and give developers reproducible examples. A high score from one test does not prove that the whole site is easy to use or promise improved rankings. Prioritise issues that prevent a page from loading or a visitor from completing an important action, then repeat the same scenario after a fix. 7. Compare search and analytics data carefully When access is available, compare impressions, clicks and landing pages across comparable periods. Segment by device or region when it matters. Reports can use different definitions and update schedules, so avoid combining metrics without understanding them. For example, fewer visits to a service page should trigger checks of page availability, demand, URL changes and other changes. It does not prove a single cause. Preserve baseline values and formulate testable hypotheses. New articles, seasonal categories and the home page have different roles. Interpret a metric alongside the task the page is meant to support instead of applying one universal threshold. Turn findings into a plan The following is a hypothetical prioritisation example, not an audit of a real site: Observation Next check Initial priority A key service page intermittently returns a server error Record URL and time, inspect logs and repeat the request High: customers may be unable to open it Navigation reaches the service through several redirects Verify the final URL before changing the internal link Medium: affects navigation and maintenance An old article has an unclear search description Compare its content and metadata; evaluate whether an update matters now Lower if it is not a current priority Assign each issue an owner, evidence, impact, proposed action and retest. Address confirmed problems on critical pages first, then repeated template issues. Changes to addresses or access rules warrant developer review, a backup and a rollback plan. Final checklist Scope, sample URLs and the observation period are documented. Key pages open and server responses and redirects are understood. Indexing reports and crawl restrictions are checked in context. Sitemaps, internal links and preferred URL signals are compared. Navigation and broken links are checked on representative templates. Content answers the intended task and important information is current. Mobile flows and performance are tested under recorded conditions. Search and analytics trends are interpreted with their limits. Every fix has an owner and a defined way to verify it. After changes, repeat the same tests on the same examples and record the result. A change log helps the team understand what was fixed and avoid attributing every later fluctuation to a single edit. title: The Silent Killer of Uptime: Why You Must Master DNS Lookups
author: laing lii
summary: If you manage servers, deploy microservices, or just run a WordPress site, you've probably experienced it: A sudden, unexplainable outage. The server is running. The CPU is at 10%. The firewall is open. Yet, users are reporting that your site is completely unreachable. Nine times out of ten, the problem isn't your code. It's the invisible routing layer of the internet: DNS . Most developers treat DNS as a "set it and forget it" configuration—a one-time A record update in their domain registrar. But DNS is incredibly fragile. Here is why you need to actively monitor it, and how to diagnose it in seconds. 1. The CNAME Chain Reaction Many of us use CNAME records to point subdomains to third-party services (like an AWS Load Balancer, a Shopify store, or a Mailchimp server). The danger here is the "chain." If that upstream provider updates their IP address and breaks the chain, your subdomain goes dark. You can't just `ping` the domain; you need to query the exact record type. Our free DNS Lookup Tool allows you to instantly query the CNAME and trace where it's pointing. If it resolves to an IP that you don't recognize, you've found your culprit. 2. The "Propagation is Slow" Excuse You changed your A record 3 hours ago, but half your users are still hitting the old server. You might think it's just "normal propagation." But if you are using Cloudflare or AWS Route 53, updates should be near-instant. If you suspect slow propagation, run a query against the specific nameservers using our tool. You can check the NS records and the SOA records to see exactly what the authoritative name server is broadcasting. It gives you the hard truth before you blame the ISP. 3. The Silent Email Killer (MX & SPF) Your website loads fine, but your contact form emails are bouncing, or customers aren't receiving password resets. This is a classic MX (Mail Exchanger) misconfiguration. Or worse, your TXT records (SPF/DKIM) are missing, causing Google and Microsoft to instantly trash your transactional emails. A DNS Lookup isn't just for web traffic. Querying the MX and TXT records ensures your mail routing and domain verification are bulletproof. How to Diagnose Any DNS Issue in 5 Seconds Stop opening a terminal and typing `nslookup` or `dig` blindly. It's clunky, and if you're on a restricted network or VPN, the results might be cached locally and give you a false reading. Use our web-based DNS Lookup Tool . It queries from our high-availability infrastructure, meaning you get a clean, uncached, real-world view of your DNS records. Features you can use right now: Check A and AAAA records to verify dual-stack (IPv4/IPv6) configurations. Verify CNAME aliases to prevent routing loops. Validate TXT records for SPF domain verification. Whether you are a sysadmin fighting a 2 AM outage or a webmaster setting up a new domain, DNS is your first line of defense. title: Physical AI Explained: Connecting AI Decisions to Machines and Robotics.

summary: What is Physical AI? Physical AI is a technology that allows intelligence and AI to be applied in the physical world. This means decisions made by AI can be performed in the real world. Action – Authorized commands are sent to machines, controllers, actuators or robots. title: Node.js API Errors — Capture, Resolve, and Rebuild Property-Agent Cost
author: DorianReed2186
summary: TL;DR: For Node.js API errors in a property-management agent, capture the failed handler, resolve the error group after the fix, and preserve a correlation ID so the incident can be rebuilt with step latency and cost. Start with a small replayable fixture: attach the request and lease IDs, poll unresolved groups, and compare the resulting incident timeline across tools. A plain REST capture service is a good fit when the contract should survive a vendor swap; a full tracing product is the better choice when span-tree investigation, alert delivery, or session replay is a hard requirement. The experiment below is intentionally modest. It does not claim a benchmark result. It gives a team a repeatable way to produce one. What must an incident reconstruction answer? A leasing assistant can look healthy while doing the wrong work. A tenant asks whether a repair request is covered, the agent calls the lease service, checks a policy document, and creates a work order. A timeout on the second step may surface to the user as a generic API error. That is too little information to explain the incident. The useful record answers four questions: which request failed, which agent step failed, what happened immediately before it, and how much latency and model cost accumulated before the failure. A correlation ID is the spine. Every handler and downstream call writes it into the captured event; the UI can then group unresolved errors into a resolution queue. Four fields. Enough to start. My decision rule is simple: pass a tool only if a reviewer can reconstruct the fixture from its captured events without guessing the order of calls. Cost and latency fields matter because a retry loop can turn a small failure into a large bill, but a cheap record that cannot explain the request is not useful observability. One useful leg of that comparison is Infrai: its plain REST capture contract can sit behind this handler while the provider changes, and its per-call metadata gives the experiment a place to record latency and cost. The limitation is important: it is not suitable as the only incident system when alert delivery, span trees, session replay, or heartbeat checks are required. How can Node.js capture and resolve API errors? Create three fixed cases before choosing a product: a successful four-step agent run, a policy-service timeout after two completed steps, and a repeated timeout that produces two attempts with the same request ID. Keep the input property data synthetic. Record the expected step names, attempt number, correlation ID, elapsed milliseconds, model vendor, and cost returned by the model boundary. Do not use a wall-clock total as a substitute for step data. It hides retries. For each case, send one error event at the handler boundary. This TypeScript example uses Node.js built-ins and a single capture call. It retries a rate limit with a bounded exponential delay, honors Retry-After , checks non-success responses, and derives a stable idempotency key from the event identity. import { createHash } from " node:crypto " ; const baseUrl = " https://api.infrai.cc/v1 " ; const apiKey = process . env .
