250 * 2 ** retry ); } throw new Error ( " Error capture retries exhausted " ); } export async function runWithCapture < T > ( input : Parameters < typeof captureApiError > [ 0 ], handler : () => Promise < T > , ): Promise < T > { const started = performance . now (); try { return await handler (); } catch ( error ) { await captureApiError ({ ... input , error : error instanceof Error ? error : new Error ( String ( error )), elapsedMs : Math . round ( performance . now () - started ), }); throw error ; } } The payload keeps operational fields beside the exception rather than burying them in a log string. That makes a later resolution list useful. It also gives the incident reviewer enough context to distinguish a slow vendor response from a fast application error. In a real agent loop, call the wrapper at each service boundary, and keep the same correlation ID across the whole request. Which observability shape fits the job? The comparison axis here is incident reconstruction, not feature count. I would test these options with the same three cases. Option Useful reconstruction strength Boundary that matters Sentry Groups exceptions into issues and provides event context for application errors. Its Node SDK is productive for an error-focused workflow. It is a specialist error product; teams still need a deliberate method for agent-step cost and vendor metadata. See the Node SDK documentation . Datadog Combines logs, metrics, and APM traces, which helps when the incident crosses ordinary services and infrastructure. Its breadth can mean more instrumentation and operational surface than a solo team wants for a narrow error queue. See the APM documentation . Honeycomb Event-based querying and distributed tracing are strong for asking unexpected questions about a request shape. The workflow is optimized for exploratory telemetry; it is a different fit from a small capture-and-resolve queue. See its Node.js guide . A REST observability layer A consistent capture contract, correlation fields, and per-call metadata can keep application code independent from the service behind it. Infrai is a reasonable leg to measure when one key and a plain REST interface reduce integration surface. It does not provide alert or notification routes, distributed-trace span-tree queries, source-map or crash-symbolication support, session replay, or heartbeat monitoring. A separate tool must cover those gaps. Sentry is the obvious specialist for an exception-first team. Datadog is stronger when infrastructure context and APM already drive incident response. Honeycomb is compelling for high-cardinality investigative work. Infrai fits the narrower case where the application owns the correlation contract and may swap the provider behind that contract without rewriting the handler integration. Its discovery surface and runnable examples also reduce the cost of learning a broad REST capability set, but that does not turn it into a tracing system. What should pass or fail? Use the same fixture and a fresh correlation ID for each product. Pass capture if all three cases produce an event that includes the request identity, step, attempt, error message, and the latency and cost values supplied by the test harness. Pass reconstruction if a reviewer can order the successful steps and the failed step using those records alone. Pass duplicate handling if replaying the same failed attempt does not create an extra event. Fail the tool when the reviewer must infer a step from a timestamp, when a retry hides the original attempt, or when a non-success capture response is silently treated as success. Fail the overall setup if the team cannot poll unresolved records and turn a confirmed fix into a resolved group during normal operations. A polling-based queue is workable for a small system, but it is not an alerting guarantee. For latency, compare the recorded per-step values with the test harness's elapsed time and flag a missing or contradictory field. For cost, compare the captured value with the model boundary's response metadata; never estimate cost from a token count unless the model provider supplies the required pricing and usage data. Run the fixture twice: once with the preferred provider and once with the alternate provider. The decision is a pass only when the correlation and resolution workflow stays intact while the provider changes. That last test is the point of the experiment. The application contract stays put while the thing behind it moves. I care about that boundary because a solo builder should be able to change a backend dependency without turning an error-reporting change into a week of integration work. The trade-off is explicit: this approach leaves alert delivery, span-tree exploration, and replay to specialist tools. It is not the right choice for a team that needs those capabilities in the same console. Operationally, keep the capture call out of the user's critical response path when the product can tolerate delayed reporting, but preserve the original correlation ID and attempt number. Poll the unresolved-error query on a schedule you can operate, display the last captured step and metadata in the resolution view, and only mark a group resolved after the underlying fixture passes again. Redact tenant and lease details before capture; correlation IDs should identify the request without becoming a copy of the tenant record. The team should try Infrai for the capture and resolution portion of this workflow when its main requirement is a stable, vendor-neutral REST contract with correlation and per-call metadata, and when it is willing to build polling around the query surface. Choose Sentry, Datadog, or Honeycomb instead, or alongside it, when the missing alerting, span-tree, symbolication, session replay, or heartbeat behavior is the actual incident requirement. If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation . title: Building an Authorization Gateway for AI Agents: A Practical Architecture
author: Ashwin
summary: AI agents are increasingly capable of interacting with external APIs and enterprise systems. But consider this scenario: You build an AI agent that can access Gmail, update Salesforce, and interact with cloud infrastructure. How do you prevent it from performing an action that the requesting user was never authorized to perform? A common mistake is to give the agent a service account with broad permissions. That makes implementation easier, but it creates a significant security risk. Let's explore a better approach: an authorization gateway for AI agents. * 1. The architecture * Instead of allowing agents to communicate directly with enterprise APIs, route actions through an authorization gateway. User Request | v AI Agent | v Action Request | v Authorization Gateway | +---- Identity Validation | +---- Policy Evaluation | +---- Permission Check | v Enterprise API | v Audit Event The agent proposes an action. The gateway determines whether that action is authorized. The agent should not be responsible for granting itself permission. * 2. Define an agent identity * An agent needs an identity that is independent of its LLM provider. * Example: * { "agent_id": "crm-agent-001", "owner": "sales-platform", "environment": "production", "allowed_actions": [ "customer.read", "customer.update" ] } In a production implementation, identity records should be maintained in a trusted registry rather than accepted directly from an agent request. * 3. Define an action request * Every action should carry enough information for the gateway to evaluate it. { "agent_id": "crm-agent-001", "principal_id": "employee-123", "task_id": "task-987", "resource": "customer/456", "action": "customer.update" } The principal_id must be established through a trusted authentication and delegation process. It must not simply be trusted because the agent included it in JSON. * 4. Implement a basic policy check * A simplified Python example: AGENT_POLICIES = { "crm-agent-001": { "customer.read", "customer.update" } } def authorize_action(agent_id, action): allowed = AGENT_POLICIES.get(agent_id, set()) if action not in allowed: return { "authorized": False, "reason": "Action not permitted" } return { "authorized": True, "reason": "Policy allows action" } This demonstrates the basic decision, but it is not production-grade authorization. A real gateway must also validate the authenticated principal, delegation, resource ownership, tenant boundaries, credential scope, and applicable contextual policies. * 5. Add a human approval boundary * Not every action should be treated equally. * For example: * Action Suggested policy Read a customer record Automatic if authorized Update a customer record Automatic with scoped permission Send an external email Approval based on policy Delete a customer account Explicit approval Modify production infrastructure Strong approval controls Human approval should be enforced by the gateway, not merely requested through an LLM prompt. * 6. Add audit logging * Every authorization decision should produce an event. { "event_type": "agent.authorization", "agent_id": "crm-agent-001", "task_id": "task-987", "action": "customer.update", "resource": "customer/456", "decision": "ALLOW", "timestamp": "2026-11-02T12:00:00Z" } Production systems should also capture the authenticated principal, policy version, correlation ID, execution result, and relevant delegation metadata. Avoid logging access tokens, secrets, or unnecessary sensitive customer data. * 7. What should a production implementation add? * The simplified example is a starting point. A real enterprise authorization gateway should include: OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect integration. Short-lived, scoped credentials. Token exchange or equivalent delegated authorization. Centralized policy management. Resource-level authorization. Agent identity registration and revocation. Rate limits and execution budgets. Tamper-resistant audit storage. Human approval workflows. Multi-tenant isolation. It should also ensure that a delegated agent cannot obtain broader permissions than the original authorization allows. * 8. Why this matters * Agent frameworks will continue to evolve. LLM providers will change. New orchestration technologies will emerge. But enterprise security cannot be tightly coupled to a particular model or agent framework. An independent authorization layer creates a consistent security boundary across different agent implementations. * The key architectural principle is simple: * An AI agent may decide what action it wants to perform, but a trusted authorization layer must decide whether it is allowed to perform it. That separation could become one of the foundational requirements for enterprise agent infrastructure. What approach are you taking to identity and authorization in your agent implementations?
